prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its development to systematic uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye. I have tried to test it against the strongest objections raised in round 1 and it holds. Katori's magic-wavelength idea is a distinct concept: it lets many neutral atoms be interrogated at once with no Doppler or recoil shift and with the lattice light shift cancelled. The result has been confirmed independently, with clocks at RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, NIST and SYRTE agreeing near 10^-18, which is the test I apply to any claimed advance. Ye's group supplied the decisive accuracy and stability demonstrations and the many-body clock physics. In reply to Danielsson's question about what the clocks have delivered beyond a smaller error bar: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetre height differences within a single atomic sample, collective spin-exchange and SU(N) interaction effects that had to be understood to reach the accuracy, tight bounds on drifts of fundamental constants, and a new sensitivity to ultralight dark matter. These are measured facts about nature that only became accessible with this instrument. The discovery-versus-technique line has always been blurry in my own field, since much of experimental astroparticle physics is a new detector opening a window. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist and does not depend on resolving the SI second redefinition, which I treat as a consequence of the result and not a condition for awarding it. I recommend a citation that names the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly, so that it does not appear to reopen the 2005 or 2012 prizes.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 prize (frequency combs and laser precision spectroscopy) and the 2012 prize (control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks) is the real weakness, and no wording removes it completely; Mehlig is right that a citation can narrow the boundary but not erase it. I also accept that Danielsson and Mehlig hold a principled position that conceptual novelty should weigh more than metrological impact, and if the committee weights it that way B039 is the natural choice. Further, credit is not fully airtight: Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Hollberg and the ion-clock groups (Al+, Yb+) have strong priority or accuracy claims and nobody here has independently verified the chronology, so the Secretary should obtain expert reviews on this. Finally, I am an experimentalist and this candidate suits my taste for instruments; I have tried to discount for that bias, and I note that my own ranking is not the only evidence, since the opening ballots had four of eight placing B022 in their top three.

responses.point: Danielsson asks what new fact about the world a lattice clock has already delivered beyond a smaller error bar, and holds that a clock is a superb measurement but does not yet show nature doing something unexpected. He also argues that my objections to B049 apply almost equally to B028.
responses.response: His question is fair and I have answered it in my case for: resolved gravitational redshift across millimetres, many-body interaction effects inside the clock, constraints on constants and dark matter. I accept that none of these is as conceptually striking as a new organising principle, and that is the honest weight of the argument against B022. I also accept his point on parity. The attribution objections I raised against B028 and B049 are comparable, and I hold both to the same standard, which is why neither is in my preferred configuration. I would add that B049 has the more identifiable decisive instrument contributions, but I cannot call that settled until the BeppoSAX and optical priority questions are reviewed.

responses.point: Mehlig places B039 above B022 because topological band theory is a new organising principle while the clock is a refinement of the comb and ion-control lineage, and says that a clock citation cannot remove the boundary against the earlier prizes. He also says that if precision is weighted above novelty, B022 wins.
responses.response: I take his last sentence as the honest statement of what separates us, and I think it is a weighting judgement and not a disagreement about facts. On overlap I do not agree that it cannot be written around. The comb prize was for a ruler that counts optical cycles and the 2012 prize for control of single ions; neither concerns neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength, where thousands of atoms are probed with the Stark shift cancelled, which is what delivered 10^-18 stability. A citation that names the magic-wavelength lattice puts that distinction on the page. I also agree that a pending SI redefinition should not drive the vote, and I do not rely on it.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B039 first for the clear theory-experiment loop and twenty years of confirmation. He argues that within a three-name limit Kane, Mele and Molenkamp best capture the decisive sequence, and says he would not oppose B022 but would resist the idea that a cleaner credit alone makes it stronger science.
responses.response: I agree with him on that last point: clean credit is a condition for a defensible prize and not a measure of scientific depth, and I do not argue B022 is better science because of it. My case is that it is a mature discovery-enabling technique and that it passes the credit test as well. On B039 I remain unable to judge the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D allocation from my own field. His answer, that the experimental discovery is what makes a prediction a physical effect, is a reasoning I find convincing as an experimentalist. My question stands: if the committee does choose B039, the citation must be confined to the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators with the HgTe observation, and external reviewers should confirm it first.

responses.point: Kroll argues the lattice clock is a different technique from the comb or ion control, that the 10^-18 comparisons are with lattice clocks, and that the redefinition of the second does not condition the result. He also notes that single-ion clocks have competing accuracy and priority claims.
responses.response: I agree with the core of this, and I will add the qualification on single-ion clocks, which I think is a real constraint on the wording. Al+ and Yb+ clocks are competitive in systematic uncertainty, so the citation should not claim that lattice clocks alone reached 10^-18 accuracy. It should credit the lattice concept and its development, not the whole field of optical clocks. That also answers the chair question about which of the two names is essential: Katori for the magic-wavelength concept and early demonstration, Ye for taking the lattice clock to record accuracy and stability and for the many-body physics, and I would not drop either.

uncertainties: Whether the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes will be seen by external reviewers as small enough, given a citation that names the magic-wavelength lattice.
Whether Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Hollberg or the ion-clock groups have priority or contribution claims that make a two-name credit hard to defend; I have not verified the chronology.
Whether weighting conceptual novelty above metrological impact, as Danielsson and Mehlig do, is the right criterion, or whether a new measurement capability with a clean credit should rank first.
Whether the B039 allocation, with the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D work outside the trio, can be defended; I rely on colleagues for this.
The BeppoSAX versus optical-counterpart priority sequence for B049, which I would want expert reviewers to examine.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B022: I have no collaboration with or personal tie to Katori or Ye. I am a Fermi-LAT collaboration member working in astroparticle and polarimetry instrumentation, so I have field proximity to B049 and B003 and would recuse myself from B049 if it advances. As Chair I record that I moved from B049 to B022 for the scientific reasons given here and that my first-round disclosure is otherwise unchanged. I do not think a formal recusal is needed for B022, B039, B035 or B025.
